questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a written policy that says "encrypt all storage accounts" does nothing on its own. In the cloud, governance that isn't enforced through a policy engine like Azure Policy, AWS Config, or IAM is just a suggestion — expressing governance rules as enforceable, machine-readable rules instead of memos is called ________.
questions.explain: Policy-as-code is the practice of expressing governance rules as enforceable, machine-readable policy (Azure Policy definitions, AWS Config rules, IAM policy JSON) rather than relying on a written procedure that nothing actually checks.

questions.prompt: Per this course, which statement correctly describes how data-governance responsibility shifts across IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS under the shared responsibility model?
options: The provider's share of the stack grows from IaaS to SaaS, but the customer's responsibility for data classification and access-control decisions never shrinks to zero at any tier.
The provider's share of the stack grows from IaaS to SaaS, and the customer's responsibility for data classification and access-control decisions shrinks to zero once a service reaches full SaaS.
The customer's share of the stack grows from IaaS to SaaS, while the provider takes on more of the data classification responsibility as services become more managed.
Responsibility is split exactly 50/50 at every tier, regardless of whether the service is IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS.
Under SaaS, the provider becomes responsible for deciding which data is sensitive, since it already runs the entire stack on the customer's behalf.
The shared responsibility model only applies to IaaS; PaaS and SaaS services are fully secured by the provider with no customer obligations.
questions.explain: The provider's share of the infrastructure stack does grow as you move from IaaS to PaaS to SaaS, but data classification and access-control decisions stay with the customer at every tier, without exception — the provider can supply encryption and strong IAM primitives, but it can never decide for you which data is sensitive or who should see it.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B matches option A's opening clause exactly and is tempting for that reason, but it swaps the one detail that matters: it claims customer responsibility for data classification and access control 'shrinks to zero' at full SaaS. The lesson is explicit that this responsibility never fully transfers, at any service tier, which is exactly why 'the cloud provider handles security' is called a dangerous half-truth.

questions.prompt: Match each level of Azure's resource hierarchy to its closest AWS Organizations counterpart, per this course.
right: Organizational unit / OU (AWS) — the closest AWS equivalent for grouping accounts under policy
Account (AWS) — the hard billing and access-control boundary equivalent
Has no real AWS equivalent in this hierarchy
The actual resource itself — the same bottom-level concept in AWS
questions.explain: Management groups group subscriptions the way OUs group accounts; subscriptions and accounts are both the hard billing/access boundary in their respective clouds; Azure's resource group — a lifecycle container for resources deployed and deleted together — has no real AWS equivalent; and an individual resource is the same bottom-level concept in both clouds.

questions.prompt: An engineer loosens a storage account's network rule at 2am to debug an incident, fixes the underlying bug, but never reverts the network rule. Six weeks later, nobody remembers it's still loosened. Per this course, what kind of policy drift is this, and why?
options: Manual override drift — a one-off direct change was made and never reverted, so the resource's actual configuration no longer matches what governance policy says it should be
Policy gap drift — the existing policy never anticipated this resource type or deployment pattern in the first place
Compliance state — this isn't drift at all, since Azure Policy would have blocked the change automatically the moment it happened
Guardrail failure — this kind of drift only happens at organizations with no landing zone at all
questions.explain: This is manual override drift: someone with sufficient permissions made a direct, one-off change (loosening a network rule to debug something) and never reverted it. Policy gap drift is the other kind — a new resource type or pattern that existing policy simply never anticipated — which isn't what happened here.

questions.prompt: Select every statement below that correctly reflects this course's view of governance across dev, test, staging, and production environments.
options: Sandbox and dev environments can loosen restrictions on what resources can be created, but should not get an exception from mandatory encryption or public-network-exposure guardrails
Staging/test governance should mirror production closely, since staging's whole purpose is catching problems before they reach production
"Non-production" is a safe synonym for "ungoverned," since real customer data should never end up in a dev or test environment
Production requires the tightest controls: least-privilege access, mandatory encryption, full audit logging, and change approval workflows
Every environment needs completely different governance principles from the others, not just a different intensity of the same principles
questions.explain: Dev/sandbox can loosen convenience restrictions but not core security guardrails; staging should mirror production closely because that's the point of staging; and production gets the tightest controls of all. "Non-production" is explicitly NOT a safe synonym for "ungoverned" — the lesson notes real customer data regularly ends up in dev/test through copies, debugging, and sample exports. And every environment shares the same governance principles; only the intensity legitimately differs.

questions.prompt: Put Azure's resource hierarchy in order, from the top-level container down to an individual resource.
questions.explain: Azure's hierarchy runs top to bottom: management groups group subscriptions so policy and access apply once and inherit downward; subscriptions are the billing/access boundary; resource groups are a logical container for resources sharing a lifecycle; and resources are the actual VMs, storage accounts, and databases at the bottom.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a ________ is anything that can be granted permissions — a human user, a group of users, an application, or a service identity.
questions.explain: A principal is the shared vocabulary term, used identically across Entra ID, Azure RBAC, and AWS IAM, for anything that can be granted permissions: a user, a group, an application, or a service identity (a managed identity in Azure, an assumed role in AWS).

questions.prompt: A governance lead needs to assign the Purview Administrator role to a new data steward so that steward can administer Purview's governance tooling itself. Which Azure service handles this assignment, and why?
options: Microsoft Entra ID — Purview Administrator is a tenant-wide directory role, not a resource-scoped Azure RBAC role
Azure RBAC — because it governs what an identity can do at the subscription scope, and Purview is deployed inside a subscription
AWS IAM — directory roles for Purview are managed through AWS, since Purview can also scan AWS sources
Azure Policy — because granting a role is treated as a policy-as-code operation
questions.explain: Directory-level roles like Purview Administrator and Compliance Administrator live in Microsoft Entra ID, which governs the tenant itself — not in Azure RBAC, which governs what an identity can do to a specific resource, resource group, subscription, or management group.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement below about Azure RBAC, per this course.
options: A role assignment made at the resource-group level applies automatically to every resource inside it
Azure RBAC's built-in roles are split into job function roles and privileged administrator roles
The Add role assignment wizard has three tabs, in order: Role, Members, and Review + assign
Azure RBAC assignments can be made directly on the Microsoft Entra tenant as a whole, the same way directory roles can
Owner and Contributor are examples of job function roles, since they are among the most commonly assigned roles
questions.explain: Scope inheritance means a resource-group assignment applies to everything inside it; the Role tab splits built-ins into job function roles and privileged administrator roles; and the wizard's three tabs run Role, Members, Review + assign in that order. Azure RBAC assignments live on resources, resource groups, subscriptions, or management groups — never on the tenant as a whole, which is Entra ID's job. And Owner/Contributor are privileged administrator roles, not job function roles.

questions.prompt: Given the IAM policy above, which of the following is this identity explicitly NOT permitted to do, under any circumstance this policy allows?
options: Delete an object in governed-data-bucket
Read an object in governed-data-bucket over HTTPS
List the contents of governed-data-bucket
Read an object in governed-data-bucket when the request is made over a secure transport
questions.explain: The policy's Action list contains only s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket — reading and listing. There is no s3:DeleteObject (or any write/delete action) anywhere in the Action list, so this identity cannot delete anything in this bucket under any circumstance this policy allows, exactly the point of a narrowly scoped least-privilege policy.

questions.prompt: Match each access governance pattern to its correct description, per this course.
right: A pre-provisioned, highly privileged credential kept in reserve for when normal access is unavailable, governed differently and audited after every use
A recurring, structured process where a resource owner periodically confirms whether someone's access is still needed
Assigning access to a group rather than an individual, so membership changes automatically grant or revoke access with no extra configuration
Defaulting to the narrowest built-in role that gets the job done, rather than a broad administrative role
questions.explain: Group-based assignment means membership changes alone grant or revoke access. Least privilege means defaulting to the narrowest job-function role. An access review is a recurring, structured re-confirmation of need. A break-glass account is deliberately excluded from all three patterns, since its entire purpose is working when the normal identity system doesn't.

questions.prompt: A script needs to call AWS APIs from an EC2 instance. Per this course's governance guidance, which approach is correct, and why?
options: Have the EC2 instance assume an IAM role via STS, producing temporary credentials that expire automatically
Create a dedicated IAM user for the script and embed its long-lived access key directly in the instance's code
Use the AWS account's root user credentials, since the root user can call every API the script might ever need
Disable IAM on the instance entirely so no credentials are required for any API call
questions.explain: AWS's current best-practice guidance prefers roles — assumed via STS, producing temporary credentials that expire on their own — over long-lived IAM user access keys. A leaked long-lived key is a standing risk until someone notices and revokes it; a role's temporary credentials bound the damage window automatically.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in ADLS Gen2, Read and Write permissions on a folder only work for a principal that also has ________ permission on every parent directory, including the container root.
questions.explain: Execute permission is what lets a principal traverse into a directory at all, independent of what it can do once there. An ACL entry granting Read on a nested folder does nothing if that identity lacks Execute on every parent directory above it, including the container root.

questions.prompt: An AWS account has Block Public Access fully enabled at the account level. An engineer then disables Block Public Access on one specific bucket within that account, intending to make it public. What actually happens?
options: The bucket remains non-public — S3 always applies the most restrictive combination of account-level and bucket-level settings, and the account-level setting still wins
The bucket becomes public, since bucket-level settings always override account-level settings
The change is blocked outright, and the engineer receives an error before the bucket-level setting can even be changed
The bucket becomes public only for requests made over HTTPS
questions.explain: S3 always applies the most restrictive combination of bucket-level and account-level Block Public Access settings. If the account has BPA fully on, a single bucket cannot opt back out of it by turning off its own bucket-level BPA — the account-level setting still wins.

questions.prompt: Match each cataloging term to its correct description, per this course.
right: The AWS process that infers schema from files and writes or updates table definitions
A Purview hierarchy for organizing sources and scoping permissions
Tells the catalog a data source exists and which collection it belongs to, without yet extracting metadata
The process that walks a registered source, extracts schema and file metadata, and can apply classification rules
questions.explain: Registering a source tells Purview it exists, without extracting anything yet. Scanning is what actually walks the source and extracts metadata, optionally classifying it. A Glue crawler is AWS's equivalent of a Purview scan. A Purview collection organizes sources and scopes permissions, closest to a Glue database.

questions.prompt: An analytics IAM role needs Select granted on a table, but its ssn column must never be visible to that role. Which AWS Lake Formation data-permission option correctly achieves this?
options: Simple column-based access, with ssn placed on the exclude list
All data access, combined with a separate IAM policy attached elsewhere that blocks the ssn column
Advanced cell-level filters, restricting only which rows are visible, not which columns
Granting Select with the Grantable permissions box checked specifically for the ssn column
questions.explain: Simple column-based access restricts Select to a chosen include- or exclude-list of columns — exactly what's needed to keep ssn hidden while still granting Select on the rest of the table. All data access grants everything with no column restriction, cell-level filters restrict rows (and can also restrict columns, but that's not what's asked here), and Grantable permissions is about re-granting a permission to someone else, not restricting it.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement below about the AWS Glue Data Catalog, per this course.
options: A Glue database is a logical namespace that holds no data itself
Deleting a Glue table also deletes the underlying S3 objects it was describing
Glue crawlers run continuously by default, scanning sources in real time
A table's schema version history is tracked automatically every time the schema changes
Schema comments can carry sensitivity classification annotations, such as "Sensitive Data Element"
questions.explain: A Glue database is just a logical namespace holding no data itself. Schema version history tracks automatically on every change. Comments on schema fields can carry classification output from automated sensitive-data detection. Deleting a Glue table does NOT delete the S3 data it described — they're separate things. And crawlers don't run continuously by default; they run on demand or on a configured schedule.

questions.prompt: A Glue table's Location field reads s3://analytics-raw/orders/. What does this confirm about the table?
options: The table is pure metadata describing data that physically lives in S3 — not a copy of the data itself
The table's underlying data has been copied into the Glue Data Catalog for faster querying
The table can no longer be queried by Amazon Athena, since Athena requires its own internal storage
The S3 objects at that path will be automatically deleted if the Glue table is ever deleted
questions.explain: A Glue table is metadata — schema, column types, partition structure, and a storage location — describing data that lives elsewhere, almost always S3. The Location field pointing to an s3:// path confirms this directly: the table and the underlying data are two separate things.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a ________ key is one an organization creates and fully controls — able to rotate on its own schedule, restrict access to with its own policy, and revoke, which immediately makes everything encrypted under it unreadable.
questions.explain: A customer-managed key (CMK) is the key-ownership tier an organization fully owns and controls. Its defining governance property is revocation — revoking it instantly makes every object encrypted under it unreadable, anywhere, which is why regulated workloads frequently mandate this specific tier.

questions.prompt: Per this course, why is "is data encrypted at rest" no longer the interesting governance question in either cloud?
options: Because encryption at rest is applied automatically by default on major storage services in both clouds, so the real governance question is who controls the key that encrypts it.

Because encryption at rest is applied automatically by default on major storage services in both clouds, so the real governance question is which compliance framework the organization has chosen to follow.
Because neither cloud supports encryption at rest anymore, having fully replaced it with key-based access control instead.
Because customer-managed keys are no longer available in either cloud, leaving only provider-managed encryption as an option.
Because encryption at rest only applies to databases, not to object storage services like S3 or Azure Blob Storage.
Because major compliance frameworks like SOC 2 explicitly forbid encrypting data that must remain fully auditable.
questions.explain: Both clouds now encrypt data at rest by default across major storage services, with no action required. That default has shifted the real governance question away from whether data is encrypted and onto who controls the key — because the key is what determines who can revoke access instantly and who satisfies a given compliance framework's key-custody requirements.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B repeats option A's opening clause word for word, which is what makes it the closest wrong answer — but it swaps out the actual conclusion. The lesson's point is specifically that the real question becomes who controls the key, not which compliance framework applies; compliance frameworks are a separate topic covered in the very next lesson, not the answer to this one.

questions.prompt: This service control policy is attached to an OU containing several production accounts. Why is it effective even against a future IAM policy mistake or a compromised credential inside those accounts?
options: Because an SCP sets a permission ceiling that no identity-based IAM policy in those accounts can ever exceed, no matter how permissive that policy is
Because SCPs automatically rotate every IAM credential in the affected accounts once a week
Because this SCP also applies to the organization's management account, which oversees every other account
Because CloudTrail itself ignores any Deny statement that doesn't originate from a service control policy
questions.explain: An SCP is a ceiling, never a grant — it narrows what any IAM policy in the covered accounts is allowed to permit, holding even against a future mistake or a compromised IAM policy. SCPs never apply to the management account itself, only to member accounts, which is the opposite of option C.

questions.prompt: A governance team wants a specific diagnostic setting automatically deployed to any new storage account that's missing it — not just flagged for review, actually remediated without a human stepping in. Which Azure Policy effect fits this requirement?
options: DeployIfNotExists
Audit
Deny
Disabled
questions.explain: DeployIfNotExists automatically remediates by deploying a compliant configuration when a resource doesn't already have one. Audit only flags a non-compliant resource without changing it, and Deny blocks the operation outright rather than fixing anything after the fact — neither matches "automatically remediate."

questions.prompt: Select every true statement below about AWS Organizations service control policies (SCPs), per this course.
options: A service control policy sets the maximum available permissions, acting as a ceiling rather than a grant
SCPs apply to every account in the organization, including the management account
The net effective permission ceiling for an account is the intersection of every SCP that applies to it — directly attached, plus every one inherited from parent OUs
Every account starts with the default FullAWSAccess SCP attached, which permits everything until replaced or supplemented
An SCP can grant a permission that no identity-based IAM policy in the account has explicitly allowed
questions.explain: SCPs are a ceiling, never a grant — they can only narrow what's possible, never widen it, so an SCP can never grant a permission an IAM policy didn't already allow. The net ceiling for an account is the intersection of every applicable SCP. Every account starts with FullAWSAccess. SCPs never apply to the management account, only to member accounts.

questions.prompt: By default, do Azure's Activity Log and AWS CloudTrail's Event history record control-plane operations, data-plane operations, or both?
options: Control-plane operations only — management operations like creating, updating, or deleting resources; data-plane activity like reading a row requires separate, opt-in logging
Data-plane operations only — every row read or object retrieved, but not resource configuration changes
Both control-plane and data-plane operations, fully, with no additional configuration required
Neither — both logs only record failed operations, never successful ones
questions.explain: Both logs track control-plane operations (create, update, delete) by default. Data-plane operations — reading a row, getting an object — require separate, opt-in logging in both clouds; they're not captured automatically.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: when the same governance rule ends up enforced with different strictness on one cloud than another, simply because maintaining two parallel rule sets is more work than maintaining one and the second one falls behind, this course calls that ________.
questions.explain: Policy drift is the central risk of running two clouds under one governance program — it isn't usually a decision, it's the result of two independent backlogs nobody is explicitly comparing.

questions.prompt: Select every area named in this course as one of the four places multi-cloud governance typically breaks down.
options: Identity
Policy enforcement
Catalogs
Audit logs
Billing and cost allocation
Physical data-center security
questions.explain: The four places named are identity, policy enforcement, catalogs, and audit logs — each one governed by separate, cloud-specific tooling that doesn't share data across providers by default. Billing/cost allocation and physical data-center security are real concerns but aren't the four governance breakdown points this lesson names.

questions.prompt: Why does Microsoft Purview's AWS S3 connector authenticate using a federated IAM role trust with an External ID, rather than a stored AWS access key?
options: Because it avoids holding a long-lived AWS credential at all — the role can only be assumed by Purview's scanning service, and the External ID prevents anyone else who learns the account ID from assuming it
Because AWS no longer supports access keys for any service as of this course's writing
Because a stored access key would lack permission to read S3 objects, regardless of the IAM policy attached to it
Because federated role trusts authenticate faster than access keys, which was the deciding factor behind this design
questions.explain: A federated IAM role trust means Purview never holds a stored, long-lived AWS credential — it authenticates by assuming a role that trusts a specific Microsoft account ID, gated by an External ID so only Purview's actual scanner (not anyone who merely learns the account ID) can assume it.

questions.prompt: A nightly job copies data from an S3 bucket into Azure Data Lake Storage. Both the S3 bucket and the ADLS container are already registered and scanned in Microsoft Purview. Does Purview automatically show lineage tracing that nightly copy?
options: No — cataloging both endpoints only solves discovery; lineage requires the tool doing the copy itself, such as Azure Data Factory, to be integrated with Purview and report what it moved
Yes — once both endpoints are scanned, Purview automatically infers lineage between any two assets that share a matching schema
Yes, but only if both assets happen to carry the same classification label
No — Purview cannot track lineage at all, even for pipelines that stay entirely within a single cloud
questions.explain: Scanning both sources catalogs each side independently; it doesn't connect the dots between them. Lineage across that hop only appears if the tool actually performing the copy is itself integrated with Purview and reports what it moved — cross-cloud lineage has to be deliberately wired up pipeline by pipeline, never assumed just because both endpoints are cataloged.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of building a multi-cloud governance control map, per this course's practice lab, in the correct order.
items: Pick your scenario: identify which cloud is primary, which is secondary, and why the secondary footprint exists
Map identity: pair the primary cloud's identity control with the secondary cloud's control and the translation mechanism
Map storage, catalog, and policy enforcement controls the same way
Map audit logging and name an owner responsible for keeping both sides in sync
Self-check the finished map against which rows would survive a primary-cloud change without anyone updating the secondary cloud by hand
questions.explain: The lab runs in exactly this order: pick the scenario first, then map identity, then storage/catalog/policy, then audit logging plus an owner for each row, and finally self-check the whole map against the real policy-drift risk — which rows depend on someone remembering to update the other side by hand.

questions.prompt: Match each chapter of this course to how it was actually applied in the Briarcliff Outdoor Gear case study.
right: Documented the shared responsibility model for both clouds side by side and treated the AWS footprint as its own landing zone needing the same dev/staging/production discipline
Set up a federation trust so Entra ID became the one identity source of truth, with AWS IAM roles granted through that trust instead of standalone AWS logins
Registered the AWS S3 buckets into the existing Purview catalog via the multicloud scanning connector, so one search covered customer data on both clouds
Wrote the encryption and access-review requirements once as an Azure Policy initiative, then translated them into an equivalent AWS Organizations service control policy
questions.explain: Chapter 1's architecture concepts (shared responsibility, landing zones) were applied first; Chapter 2's identity patterns set up one federated identity source; Chapter 3's cataloging united both clouds' data under one searchable Purview catalog; and Chapter 4's policy/encryption controls were written once and deliberately translated to the secondary cloud, closing exactly the policy-drift gap Chapter 5 warns about.
